entities.summary:
Shepseskaf was a pharaoh of ancient Egypt, the sixth and probably last ruler of the Fourth Dynasty during the Old Kingdom period. He reigned most probably for four but possibly up to seven years in the late 26th to mid-25th century BC. His reign is notable for the construction of the Second Pyramid of Giza, one of the largest pyramids ever built, and the establishment of a new system of governance. The pyramid's construction required the labor of thousands of skilled workers, who were likely slaves or peasants. This system of governance would later be adopted by other pharaohs and empires, shaping the course of Egyptian and Mediterranean history. Shepseskaf's legacy is also marked by the decline of the Old Kingdom period, which was eventually succeeded by the First Intermediate Period. The instability of this period would have far-reaching consequences for Egyptian politics and society, paving the way for the rise of new dynasties and the eventual reunification of Egypt.

Shepseskaf's tomb was discovered in 1954, and it is believed to have been buried with a treasure trove of gold and other precious objects. The tomb's discovery provided valuable insights into the life and reign of Shepseskaf, including the presence of a number of artifacts that were previously unknown. The discovery of Shepseskaf's tomb has been hailed as one of the greatest archaeological discoveries of the 20th century, shedding new light on the history of ancient Egypt.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Shepseskaf's reign was significant for the construction of the Second Pyramid of Giza and the establishment of a new system of governance, which would later be adopted by other pharaohs and empires. His legacy is also marked by the decline of the Old Kingdom period and the instability of the First Intermediate Period.
